tip: In the present perfect the participle lands at the very end, so gehoord follows both hebben and niets.
For the future, zullen takes a plain infinitive and pushes it to the end: zullen ... schoonmaken.
Zal is the singular of zullen; use zal with hij, zij or ik, and zullen with wij or a plural subject.
How-are-you is fixed as hoe gaat het met je, literally how goes it with you; je is the casual you.
When an adverb like helaas opens the sentence, the verb comes before the subject: helaas kan ik, not helaas ik kan.
Niet sits just before the closing infinitive, so it lands right ahead of oplossen at the end.
After een with a de-word the adjective takes -e, and tuin is a de-word, so you get een mooie tuin.
Meisje is grammatically neuter, so it is het meisje, not de, even though it means girl.
Half negen means 8:30, not 9:30; Dutch half X counts half an hour before X, not after.
Chasing wraps around the noun: achter goes before the kat and aan after it, giving achter de kat aan.
With een plus a het-word the adjective stays bare, so it is een mooi boek, not mooie, since boek is het.
Use geen, not niet, to negate a noun without the: geen tijd means no time or not any time.
Last hebben van means to be bothered by, and nergens replaces the object: nergens last van is bothered by nothing.
Dutch marks an upright position with staan, so a bike staat in de schuur where English just says is.
Comparatives add -er and pair with dan for than: moeilijker dan verwacht means harder than expected.
After a linking verb like is, the adjective stays uninflected, so it stays zacht, never zachte.
Before a plural noun the adjective always takes -e, so ramen gives grote ramen.
In a wat-clause the verb moves to the end, so it is wat je bedoelt, not wat bedoel je.
Gaan plus an infinitive expresses a near-future plan, like going to: ga ... kijken is am going to watch.
The superlative adds -ste after de, so lekker becomes de lekkerste, meaning the tastiest.
A short vowel doubles the final consonant in the plural, so vis becomes vissen, not visen.
Most ordinals up to nineteen add -de, so vijf becomes vijfde for fifth.
In a separable verb's participle the ge- slots between prefix and stem, so inpakken becomes ingepakt.
Currency and measure words stay singular after a number, so it is veertigduizend euro, never euros.
Diminutives form their plural with -s, so bordje becomes bordjes, not bordjen.
Dutch uses the plain present for the future when a time word is there, so komt with morgen means will come.
Vertrekken is a strong verb, so its past changes the vowel: vertrekken becomes vertrok, not vertrekte.
Mogen means to be allowed to, so mag je marks permission, not ability the way kan je would.
A doubled long vowel drops to single when the syllable opens in the plural, so boom becomes bomen.
In the passive, door marks who does the action, so geschreven door de dichter means written by the poet.
Dutch pairs the plain present with al for something ongoing, so staat al eeuwen means has stood for centuries.
Yes/no questions start with the verb, so it is Heeft u ...?, with the subject after the verb.
Even softens a request into just a moment or real quick, so helpen with even sounds lighter than a bare helpen.
By a vehicle is met de plus the vehicle, so met de trein means by train, not per or op.
For an animal in a spot Dutch prefers zitten, so the kat zit op het dak where English says sits or is.
With a superlative, van means in, so de grootste van Europa means the largest in Europe.
To consist of is bestaan uit, always paired with uit, so de salade bestaat uit lists its parts.
Want means because but keeps normal word order, so want het is benauwd, unlike omdat which sends the verb to the end.
For time ahead, over means in or from now, so over vijf minuten means in five minutes.
Starting a clause with dan flips subject and verb, so it is dan zie je, not dan je ziet.
Dutch drops the word for of in quantities, so a glass of wine is simply een glas rode wijn.
Zich afvragen means to wonder and needs the reflexive me, so it is ik vraag me af, not ik vraag af.
For in order to, wrap the infinitive in om ... te, so om bij het centrum te komen means to reach the center.
Dutch says the unit before the ten, so 55 is vijfenvijftig, literally five-and-fifty.
Weak verbs form the past with -te or -de, so bedanken becomes bedankte for thanked.
Verbs of change take zijn, not hebben, in the perfect, so it is zijn verwelkt for have wilted.
Dutch adverbs use the plain adjective with no -ly ending, so langzaam covers both slow and slowly.
Te koop is a set phrase for on the market, so is te koop means is for sale, not literally to buy.
